pathophysiology.summary: Extrapulmonary tuberculosis (EPTB) is Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection outside the lung parenchyma and makes up a large share of TB notified in India. Bacilli spread from a primary focus through lymphatics and blood and form granulomas in lymph nodes (the commonest site, often cervical), pleura, peritoneum and bowel, meninges, bones and joints. Disease is paucibacillary, so smear and culture yields are low and molecular tests vary by specimen; tissue or fluid from the affected site should be sent for nucleic acid amplification testing (NAAT), culture and histology, and every patient tested for HIV. TB meningitis is the most dangerous form: basal exudate causes hydrocephalus, cranial nerve palsies, vasculitic infarcts and coma, and treatment must start without waiting for proof. India uses the same daily fixed-dose combination regimen as for pulmonary TB, 2 months of isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol (2HRZE) followed by isoniazid, rifampicin and ethambutol (HRE), for 6 months in total for lymph node, pleural and abdominal disease, and extended to 12 months with adjunctive corticosteroids for TB meningitis.
keyMechanisms: Haematogenous and lymphatic spread seeds lymph nodes, serosae and meninges.
Granulomatous inflammation with caseation causes nodes, effusions, ascites and strictures.
Basal meningeal exudate causes hydrocephalus, infarcts and cranial nerve palsies; steroids reduce this inflammation.
Paucibacillary disease lowers test sensitivity, so clinical diagnosis is common.

pathophysiology.summary: Drug-resistant TB arises when M. tuberculosis carries mutations that defeat key drugs, either acquired through incomplete treatment or transmitted directly. India has the world's largest number of cases. Rifampicin-resistant TB (RR-TB) and multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB, resistant to isoniazid and rifampicin) do not respond to the standard regimen; pre-extensively drug-resistant TB (pre-XDR) adds fluoroquinolone resistance, and XDR-TB adds bedaquiline or linezolid resistance. NTEP tests every presumptive TB patient by molecular testing for rifampicin resistance, then tests rifampicin-resistant patients for isoniazid and fluoroquinolone resistance, with liquid culture testing of newer drugs. Since 2024 the all-oral 6-month regimen of bedaquiline, pretomanid, linezolid and moxifloxacin (BPaLM) is first choice for eligible patients aged 14 or older; a 9–11-month shorter oral regimen is used for children under 14 and some ineligible patients, and an 18–20-month longer oral regimen for the rest. The main toxicities are QT prolongation (bedaquiline, moxifloxacin) and myelosuppression, neuropathy and optic neuritis (linezolid), which need scheduled monitoring.
keyMechanisms: Chromosomal mutations (for example rpoB for rifampicin) confer resistance.
Incomplete or interrupted treatment selects resistant strains; transmission spreads them.
Bedaquiline targets mycobacterial ATP synthase; pretomanid and linezolid add bactericidal activity.
Linezolid inhibits mitochondrial protein synthesis, causing marrow, nerve and optic toxicity.

pathophysiology.summary: TB preventive treatment treats TB infection before it progresses to disease, which is a pillar of India's TB elimination strategy. People recently infected (household contacts of pulmonary TB) and people with weakened immunity (people living with HIV, those starting anti-TNF or other immunosuppressive treatment, dialysis, silicosis, transplant candidates) carry the highest risk of progression. Before TPT, active TB must be excluded by symptom screening and, where available, chest X-ray, because giving a one- or two-drug preventive regimen to someone with active disease risks resistance. TB infection testing (tuberculin skin test or interferon-gamma release assay) is offered to contacts aged 5 and over and other risk groups where available, but TPT must not be delayed when tests are unavailable. India offers several regimens: daily isoniazid for 6 months (6H), daily rifampicin with isoniazid for 3 months (3RH) for under-15s, weekly isoniazid with rifapentine for 3 months (3HP), daily isoniazid with rifapentine for 1 month (1HP) from age 13, and 6 months of levofloxacin (6Lfx) for contacts of fluoroquinolone-sensitive MDR/RR-TB.
keyMechanisms: Latent bacilli can reactivate, especially with immune suppression or recent infection.
Preventive drugs kill the small bacillary population of TB infection.
Single or dual drugs are inadequate for active disease, so disease must be excluded first.
Rifamycins induce liver enzymes, causing interactions with antiretrovirals and opioid substitution.

symptoms: Any cough, fever, night sweats or weight loss suggests active TB and excludes TPT until evaluated

pathophysiology.summary: HIV infects CD4 T lymphocytes and, without treatment, progressively destroys cellular immunity, leading to opportunistic infections and cancers. India has one of the world's largest populations living with HIV, served through NACO's integrated counselling and testing centres and antiretroviral therapy (ART) centres. Diagnosis uses a national strategy of two or three rapid tests with different antigens. Advanced HIV disease (CD4 below 200 cells/mm³ or a WHO stage 3–4 event, and all children under 5 not on ART) carries high early mortality, mainly from TB and cryptococcal meningitis, so it triggers a package of screening and prophylaxis. Tuberculosis is the commonest opportunistic infection and cause of death in people with HIV. Lifelong dolutegravir-based ART suppresses viral replication, restores immunity and prevents transmission. In TB-HIV, ART starts within 2 weeks of TB treatment (4–8 weeks in TB meningitis), and dolutegravir is given twice daily with rifampicin because rifampicin lowers dolutegravir levels. Viral load below 1,000 copies/mL defines suppression.
keyMechanisms: HIV depletes CD4 T cells, impairing cell-mediated immunity.
Low CD4 counts permit TB, cryptococcal and other opportunistic infections.
ART suppresses replication and allows immune recovery; early ART can trigger immune reconstitution inflammation.
Rifampicin induces enzymes that lower dolutegravir and protease-inhibitor levels.

pathophysiology.summary: Leprosy is a chronic infection by Mycobacterium leprae, spread by respiratory droplets from untreated patients during close prolonged contact; India reports the largest number of new cases worldwide. The organism grows slowly in cooler tissues and has affinity for Schwann cells in peripheral nerves. Host immunity shapes disease: strong cell-mediated immunity gives few hypopigmented anaesthetic patches (paucibacillary, PB), weak immunity gives many lesions, nodules and high bacterial loads (multibacillary, MB). Nerve damage causes loss of sensation, thickened nerves and weakness, which lead to injuries, ulcers and deformity; immune reactions during or after treatment can rapidly damage nerves. Diagnosis rests on at least one of three cardinal signs: a patch with definite sensory loss, a thickened peripheral nerve with sensory or motor loss, or acid-fast bacilli on slit-skin smear. All patients now receive three-drug MDT (rifampicin, dapsone, clofazimine) for 6 months (PB) or 12 months (MB). Contacts aged 2 and over receive single-dose rifampicin prophylaxis once leprosy and TB are excluded.
keyMechanisms: M. leprae infects Schwann cells and macrophages in cool tissues.
Host cell-mediated immunity determines paucibacillary versus multibacillary disease.
Peripheral nerve damage causes anaesthesia, weakness and secondary injury.
Immune reactions cause acute neuritis and skin inflammation.

pathophysiology.summary: Children develop TB after infection from an adult with pulmonary TB, usually in the household, and young children progress quickly to disease, including severe disseminated (miliary) and meningeal forms. Disease in children is paucibacillary and children cannot easily produce sputum, so diagnosis relies on history (cough or fever for 2 weeks or more, weight loss or failure to thrive, contact), chest X-ray, and molecular testing of sputum, induced sputum or gastric aspirate; many children are treated as clinically diagnosed. Tuberculin skin testing only supports and never alone diagnoses TB, and interferon-gamma release assays are not recommended in the national workflow. Treatment uses flavoured dispersible fixed-dose combinations dosed by weight band: 2 months of isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol followed by 4 months of isoniazid, rifampicin and ethambutol for most forms, extended to 12 months for TB meningitis and osteoarticular disease, with steroids for meningitis and selected severe intrathoracic disease.
keyMechanisms: Recent household infection leads to rapid progression in young children.
Poor containment causes miliary and meningeal disease.
Paucibacillary disease and poor sputum production lower test yield.
Granulomatous inflammation causes nodes, effusions and meningeal exudate.

clinicalManagement.title: Suspect and test
actions: Ask about cough or fever for 2 weeks or more, weight loss and household contact.
Chest X-ray; NAAT on sputum, induced sputum or gastric aspirate; HIV test.
Give amoxicillin or amoxicillin–clavulanate (not quinolones or linezolid) and reassess.
Treat as clinically diagnosed TB.

clinicalManagement.title: Treat with weight-band dispersible FDCs
actions: Most forms: 2HRZE then 4HRE.
TB meningitis and osteoarticular TB: 2HRZE then 10HRE.
Steroids: TB meningitis (prednisolone 2 mg/kg/day for 4 weeks then taper); consider for miliary TB with hypoxia, endobronchial TB or massive effusion with distress.

clinicalManagement.title: Monitor
actions: Check dose by current weight, adherence and tolerance; NAAT is not used to track progress.
Post-treatment review at 6, 12, 18 and 24 months.

clinicalManagement.title: Refer
actions: Uncertain diagnosis, suspected drug resistance, no response, intolerance, surgical abdomen, compressive myelopathy, or deteriorating meningitis.

teaching.scope: Tuberculosis in children in India: when to suspect, specimens and NAAT, chest X-ray-led algorithm, weight-band dispersible regimens, durations by site, steroids and referral.
learningObjectives: Suspect TB from symptoms, growth and contact history.
Use chest X-ray and NAAT on appropriate specimens.
Dose by weight band and extend for meningitis and bone TB.
keyPoints: Negative NAAT does not exclude TB in children.
Tuberculin test alone never starts treatment.
pitfalls: Using IGRA or pleural ADA, which the workflow advises against.
Not adjusting dose as the child gains weight.
Missing contacts and TPT for siblings.
